title: Heart Attacks in Your 20s and 30s: Why India's Young Are Dying of a Disease Their Grandparents Survived
excerpt: Cardiologists warn that half of all heart attacks in Indian men now occur before the age of 50, driven by a toxic combination of sedentary lifestyles, chronic stress, and genetic predisposition.
body:
• 50% of heart attacks in Indian men now occur before the age of 50, with 25% striking before 40, according to the Indian Heart Association
  • Heart attack deaths in India have risen 54% over the past decade, per National Crime Records Bureau data
  • The rate of cardiac events among Indians aged 20-30 is climbing 2% per year
  • Experts cite a "perfect storm" of sedentary lifestyles, work stress, diabetes, smoking, poor diet, and a documented genetic predisposition among South Asians

When a 28-year-old software engineer in Bengaluru collapsed during a morning run last month, his family assumed it was heatstroke. It was a massive myocardial infarction — a heart attack. He survived, but barely. His story is increasingly common, and cardiologists across India say the trend is alarming.

The Numbers

Data from the Indian Heart Association (IHA) paints a stark picture: 50% of all heart attacks in Indian men now occur before the age of 50, and a full 25% strike before 40. These are not statistical outliers — they represent a structural shift in who gets heart disease and when.

The National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) reports that heart attack deaths in India have increased 54% over the past decade. Among the 20-30 age group specifically, the rate of cardiac events is climbing approximately 2% annually, according to data compiled by Kauvery Hospital's cardiology department.

"We are seeing patients in their mid-20s with the coronary arteries of a 60-year-old. This is not an exaggeration — it is a clinical reality we encounter multiple times a week."

— Dr. Rajiv Agarwal, Kauvery Hospital

Why Indians Are Uniquely Vulnerable

Cardiologists point to a convergence of factors that make South Asians — and Indians in particular — disproportionately susceptible to early cardiac disease.

Genetic predisposition. Multiple studies have established that South Asians carry a higher baseline risk of coronary artery disease compared to other ethnic groups, independent of lifestyle factors. Indians tend to have smaller coronary arteries, higher levels of lipoprotein(a), and a greater tendency toward insulin resistance — all of which accelerate arterial plaque formation.

The modern Indian lifestyle. Urbanisation has brought a dramatic shift in how young Indians live. Long sedentary hours in IT and corporate jobs, chronic work stress amplified by always-on digital connectivity, rising diabetes rates (India has an estimated 101 million diabetics), and diets increasingly high in refined carbohydrates and trans fats have created what cardiologists describe as a "perfect storm."

Smoking and air pollution. India has over 100 million smokers, and many of its cities rank among the world's most polluted. Both are established independent risk factors for cardiovascular disease.

The Diaspora Dimension

The genetic risk follows Indians wherever they go. Studies in the US and UK have consistently shown that South Asian immigrants have 2-4 times the rate of coronary artery disease compared to the general population, even after adjusting for diet and exercise. The American Heart Association formally recognised South Asian heritage as an independent risk factor in 2022.

For NRIs, this means standard Western risk calculators often underestimate cardiac risk. Cardiologists recommend that Indians abroad begin cardiovascular screening — including lipid panels, HbA1c, and coronary calcium scoring — by age 30, rather than the standard 40-45 recommended for the general population.

What Young Indians Can Do

Experts emphasise that genetic risk is not destiny. Regular cardiovascular exercise (at least 150 minutes per week), aggressive management of blood sugar and cholesterol, stress reduction, smoking cessation, and a diet low in refined carbohydrates can dramatically reduce risk. The challenge, doctors say, is getting young people to take the threat seriously before their first event.
